prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I ranked IceCube first and the lattice clock fourth in my opening ballot, and I now put the lattice clock first. The reason is that it has the cleanest combination of the criteria across the eight ballots. It is a specific, original invention (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first realization) with an equally identifiable second contribution (Ye's route to record accuracy and many-body clock physics), so a two-name prize maps onto the history without forcing a split among many collaborators. It is reproduced in many independent laboratories and species, with comparisons at the 10^-18 level, and it underpins redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. It also has the broadest opening support in the room: five of eight members place it in their top three, including two first places, and only my own ranking put it as low as fourth. Hall and Haensch were honoured in 2005 for the comb, and Wineland in 2012 for control of single ions, but the lattice clock is a different principle (many atoms interrogated at once in a magic-wavelength trap) and is the later and distinct step.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping can look like a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that the credit sits uncomfortably close to the ion-clock and frequency-comb communities (and to groups at PTB, Paris and NIST who contributed parallel platforms). The SI second has also not yet been formally redefined, so one could argue for waiting for that milestone. Finally, a metrology invention can be judged less transformative than a new class of phases or a new observational window, and I recognise that my own move away from IceCube could simply reflect a wish not to over-promote my own field.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because it exemplifies progress through better measurement, has a natural two-person attribution (Katori proposal and realization, Ye accuracy and systematics), and is not crowded out by the earlier comb prize.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution argument and it is what moved me, since it is much firmer than for any of the larger-team candidates. I would qualify his claim that the comb prize does not crowd it: the comb is the enabling technology for reading out optical clocks, so the citation must be written around magic-wavelength trapping and the accuracy it allowed, not around optical frequency metrology in general. I also do not accept that a pending redefinition of the second is a reason for urgency; it is a supporting application, not the criterion.

responses.point: Lindroth supports the clock as original and clean, notes the atomic-physics control of light shifts, and asks whether the committee wants to separate the lattice-clock concept from the later accuracy race.
responses.response: I would keep them together. Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy and systematic control form one achievement, and splitting them would invite a priority dispute that the record does not require. Her second ballot place for Hubbard simulation (B022) is a serious competitor in atomic physics, but I find its credit allocation harder, because she herself notes that Greiner's omission is a real difficulty and that it overlaps with B008, whereas the clock does not have that problem.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first as an unusually complete theory-to-experiment chain, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credited names and that the 2016 prize is a neighbouring overlap.
responses.response: I respect the scientific strength of B016 and have kept it as my first alternative. My reservation is that the HgTe route came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the experimental credit for Molenkamp rests on a proposal the prize would leave unrecognised. Together with the 2016 topological-phases prize, I am less convinced than he is that the case is stronger than the clock. If the committee judges the BHZ omission acceptable, I would not oppose a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize.

responses.point: Mehlig puts conformal field theory first as a foundational, long-confirmed framework, calls recognition overdue, and also ranks the lattice clock third with a fair two-person attribution.
responses.response: We agree on the clock. On B001 I would press the credit problem harder than his opening does: Belavin is the founding author of the decisive 1984 paper, and a three-person prize that leaves him out is hard to defend. The experimental evidence is also indirect and limited to specific universality classes, which makes it a weaker fit to the discovery-or-invention criterion than an instrument with a measured outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how to word the citation to make that distinction.
The relative share of Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy programme, and whether other lattice-clock groups would be argued to have a claim.
Whether I have moved because of the arguments or because of the weight of colleagues' first-place votes; I have tried to rely on the attribution and confirmation arguments rather than on counts.
IceCube source-level evidence and the attribution among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the wider collaboration remain unsettled and may change my view if a stronger credit rationale is presented.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred ballot B014. My documented connections are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, none of which involves the credited atomic-physics names. B021 (IceCube) is in my own field, astroparticle physics, so I flag the proximity to colleagues, although my profile records no tie to its credited names.
